name: Petra
info: Petra is the rock-cut city in southern Jordan that the Nabataeans settled in the 4th century BCE and made their capital, a trading hub on the incense routes known for its carved sandstone façades and water systems.

facts.made: The Nabataeans, a northern Arabian people once nomadic, who settled the site in the 4th century BCE and made it their capital in the 2nd century BCE; later Roman and Byzantine builders added roads, a colonnaded street and churches
facts.form: A city in a mountain basin reached through the narrow Siq gorge, with tombs, temples and monuments carved into rose-coloured sandstone in a Nabataean version of Hellenistic style, a theatre cut into the hillside, and dams, cisterns and conduits
facts.where: In southern Jordan, on the eastern flank of the Arabah valley, managed since 2007 by the Petra Archaeological Park
facts.known: the Treasury (Al-Khazneh); the Monastery (Ad Deir); the Siq; rainwater collection and flood control; the incense trade; the traditional tomb of Aaron; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985

t: The Nabataeans' control of water, through dams, cisterns and conduits, turned a desert basin into an artificial oasis and a hub of the caravan trade.
Annexed by Rome in 106, Petra declined as sea routes took its trade and after the earthquake of 363, though papyri show the city still flourishing in the 6th century.
Long abandoned except by a handful of nomads, it was described for Europeans by Johann Ludwig Burckhardt in 1812 and is now Jordan's most visited site.
dyk: The face of the Treasury is marked by hundreds of bullet holes, made by local Bedouin who hoped to dislodge riches once rumoured to be hidden inside it.
ev: The Nabataeans settled the Petra area
Petra became the capital of the Nabataean Kingdom
The city flourished, the Treasury was built and the population peaked at an estimated 20,000
Nabataea was annexed by the Romans and became part of the province of Arabia Petraea
An earthquake destroyed many buildings and crippled the water management system
The Urn Tomb was consecrated as a church in the time of Bishop Jason
The Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt became the first European to describe the ruins
Petra was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
The area around Petra has been inhabited from as early as 7000 BCE, when some of the earliest recorded farmers settled at Beidha just to the north. Petra appears in Egyptian campaign accounts and the Amarna letters as Pel, Sela or Seir, and in the Iron Age, between 1200 and 600 BCE, the Edomites occupied the area, using its mountains as a reservoir of water and a stopping point for merchants trading wine, olive oil and wood. An Edomite site on the summit of Umm el-Biyara dates from no earlier than the 7th century BCE.

The Nabataeans were one of several nomadic Bedouin tribes of the Arabian Desert. Though at first embedded in Aramaic culture, they are identified by archaeological, religious and linguistic evidence as a northern Arabian tribe. They settled at Petra in the 4th century BCE, and Diodorus Siculus describes the expeditions Antigonus sent against them in 312 BCE, though his account implies no town yet existed there. Their own name for the city seems to have been Raqēmō; Josephus records that the Arabs of his day still called it Rekeme. Petra became the capital of the Nabataean Kingdom in the 2nd century BCE, its wealth drawn from its place on the incense trade routes.
sections.content:
Petra lies in a basin surrounded by mountains, next to Jabal Al-Madbah. Most visitors now enter from the east through the Siq, a dark gorge in places only 3–4 metres wide, formed by a split in the sandstone. At its end stands Al-Khazneh, the Treasury, 24 metres wide and 37 metres tall, its façade carved with a broken pediment around a central tholos, the twins Castor and Pollux, and a female figure believed to be Isis-Tyche. Its style refers to the architecture of Alexandria.

Beyond lie a theatre said to hold about 8,500 people, the Royal Tombs, among them the Palace, Corinthian, Silk and Urn Tombs, a pool and garden complex with an island pavilion, and the Colonnaded Street leading to the Sacred Quarter and its temples, the Qasr al-Bint and the Temple of the Winged Lions. The Monastery, Petra's largest monument at 45 metres tall and 50 metres wide, was dedicated to the deified king Obodas I. The High Place of Sacrifice on Jebel Madbah saw libations, animal sacrifice and the burning of frankincense. Most tombs hold small burial niches carved into the rock.
sections.making:
Excavations have shown that the Nabataeans' ability to control water led to the rise of the city. The area suffers flash floods, which they controlled with dams, cisterns and water conduits that stored water through long droughts and allowed the city to profit from its sale. The archaeologist Philip Hammond, who worked at Petra for nearly 40 years, believed the carved channels in the walls and ground once held ceramic pipes fed from rock-cut systems on the canyon rim.

The monuments were cut directly into the sandstone, their façades mostly in a Hellenistic style that reflects the many cultures, all influenced by Greek culture, with which the Nabataeans traded. The Monastery dates from the 1st century BCE, the Temple of the Winged Lions from the reign of Aretas IV (9 BCE–40 CE), and the Treasury, possibly the mausoleum of Aretas IV, from the 1st century CE. New evidence suggests that prominent structures were aligned with sunrises and sunsets at the equinoxes and solstices. In 2016 satellite images and drones revealed a huge platform south of the city, tentatively dated to about 150 BCE, whose ceremonial purpose is unexplained.
sections.reception:
Pliny the Elder and other writers identified Petra as the capital of the Nabataeans and the centre of their caravan trade, controlling routes to Gaza, Bosra and Damascus, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. The Nabataeans worshipped Arab gods, chief among them Dushara with Al-'Uzzā, Allat and Manāt, and some of their deified kings. After Rome annexed the kingdom in 106, Trajan built the Via Traiana Nova through the city, Hadrian visited in 130 and named it Hadriānī Petra Metropolis, and a governor raised a mausoleum for his son among the royal tombs.

Christianity reached Petra in the 4th century, and the city became the capital of the Byzantine province of Palaestina III; the Urn Tomb was consecrated as a church in 447. A tradition holds that Moses struck the rock here to bring forth water, giving Wadi Musa its name, and that Aaron is buried on nearby Jabal Haroun, a belief going back at least to Josephus; a monastery there drew pilgrims. Crusaders held the area until 1189 and built castles, and the Mamluk sultan Baibars visited the ruins towards the end of the 13th century.
sections.survival:
Petra declined as sea routes replaced the caravan trade and as Palmyra drew Arab trade away. The earthquake of 363 destroyed many buildings, yet 140 papyri found in the Byzantine Church, mostly contracts of the 530s to 590s, show the city still flourishing in the 6th century. It is not mentioned in accounts of the Muslim conquest, and by the early Islamic era it was abandoned except for a handful of nomads.

In 1812 Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, travelling in disguise, became the first European to describe it; artists such as David Roberts and Frederic Edwin Church followed. Weakened structures left tombs open to thieves. In the 1980s the Jordanian government resettled the Bedul Bedouin, who had lived in the site's caves, at Umm Sayhoun. Petra became a World Heritage Site in 1985, and conservation has addressed the Siq, the Treasury, temples, churches and wall paintings. The site faces collapse, flood erosion, salt weathering, poor restoration and heavy tourism, with 1.2 million visitors in 2019; animal welfare groups have documented the abuse of working animals.
sections.legacy:
UNESCO has called Petra 'one of the most precious cultural properties of man's cultural heritage'. It is a symbol of Jordan and the country's most visited attraction, and in a popular poll in 2007 it was named one of the New 7 Wonders of the World. The skills and heritage of the Bedouin of the area were inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage List in 2008.

The city has long held a place in writing and art. John William Burgon's prize poem of 1845 called it 'a rose-red city half as old as time', and it has appeared in novels such as Agatha Christie's Appointment with Death and the Tintin adventure The Red Sea Sharks, in the Rahbani brothers' musical Petra, and in films including Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade. For some Israeli youth of the 1950s, illicit hikes to Petra became a dangerous, sometimes deadly, rite of passage, remembered in the ballad 'The Red Rock'.

summary: Petra, in southern Jordan, was settled by the Nabataeans in the 4th century BCE and grew into their capital and a hub of the incense trade, sustained by careful control of water. After Roman annexation, earthquake and the loss of its trade it was abandoned, and since its description by Burckhardt in 1812 it has become a World Heritage Site and Jordan's most visited place.
